claims.text: Controlled multi-element mixing increases the alloy's configurational entropy.
Increased configurational entropy induces greater local lattice strain or distortion.
Increased configurational entropy broadens the phonon spectrum or phonon density of states.
Structural heterogeneity and phonon-spectrum broadening strengthen electron-phonon coupling.
Stronger electron-phonon coupling promotes Cooper-pair formation.
Cooper-pair formation produces a superconducting gap and causes superconductivity to emerge at low temperature.
The low-mixing baseline has a relatively uniform lattice and minimal atomic-scale disorder.
The low-mixing baseline lacks the enhanced electron-phonon coupling attributed to configurational entropy.
High-configurational-entropy samples will exhibit a distinct superconducting transition in the low-temperature regime.
High-configurational-entropy samples will have higher superconducting critical current density than low-mixing samples.
High-configurational-entropy samples will exhibit a measurable superconducting gap.
The clearest superconducting effects are expected between approximately 2 K and 5 K.
The proposed mechanism should operate roughly below 20 K.
The effect may depend on the precise elemental mixing ratios.
Disorder-induced electron scattering may affect the superconducting properties.

contradictions.description: The starting material is called an HEA while simultaneously being defined as a minimally mixed alloy with only one or two principal elements; the intervention then presents multi-element mixing as what creates the high-configurational-entropy state.

The experiment calls the two sets the same base composition, but one set is to contain one or two principal elements while the other receives additional multi-element mixing. The intended substitution scheme or compositional constraint is not specified, so literal composition matching is incompatible with the stated intervention.
